issues.subcategory: unsupported empirical claim
issues.description: The discussion contains a sentence asserting that findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings, but the study exclusively used single-sex chains and no mixed-gender data were collected or analyzed. This sentence also syntactically disrupts the surrounding paragraph ('Instead they mainly produce unidimensional models…'), strongly suggesting it was inserted without proper integration—possibly in response to reviewer comments—and constitutes an empirical claim unsupported by any data in the paper.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: accepting the null from an underpowered test
issues.description: The paper's central claim—that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect' on the pace of cultural evolution—is drawn from a Bayesian analysis where the 95% credible interval for the treatment effect on speed spans nearly 29 m/h, from −10.76 to +18.13 m/h. This interval is entirely compatible with practically meaningful positive or negative effects. With only 14 chains per treatment, the design lacks the statistical resolution to distinguish 'no effect' from 'moderate effect,' yet the paper repeatedly presents absence of credible evidence as positive evidence for absence, a classic error that undermines the paper's core inference.
issues.quote: Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding… Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.subcategory: causal claims from non-randomized within-treatment comparison
issues.description: The comparison of participants who inherited inertia theories versus centre-of-mass theories versus full theories is treated as though it supports causal conclusions about the effects of inheriting each theory type. However, the type of theory a participant received was entirely determined by what prior chain members happened to produce—it was never randomized. Participants who received inertia theories may differ systematically from those who received centre-of-mass theories in chain position, chain-level performance trajectory, and individual characteristics. The authors acknowledge this is an 'exploratory analysis' but still draw directional causal conclusions from it.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia theory reduces understanding about centre of mass and increases understanding about inertia, while inheriting a centre-of-mass theory increases understanding about centre of mass and reduces understanding about inertia

issues.subcategory: deviation from pre-registration due to model non-convergence
issues.description: The pre-registered model for Analysis 4 included 'Physical Principle' and 'Physical Principle × Treatment' as predictors and 'Player's identity' as a random effect. The authors report that this model failed to converge because inertia and centre-of-mass understanding scores were negatively correlated. Rather than treating this as a finding or reporting both the pre-registered and revised analyses, they replaced it with a model on aggregated scores. This eliminates precisely the between-dimension distinction that is central to the paper's later exploratory claims about inherited theory type shaping selective understanding. Model non-convergence in a pre-registered analysis is a major validity signal that warrants more than a brief footnote-style acknowledgment.
issues.quote: analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated… As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable 'Physical Principle' in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc model selection
issues.description: For Analysis 1 (preregistered), the final model was chosen by comparing multiple candidate models based on fit to the observed data. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom: the number of candidate models examined, the fit criterion used, and the stopping rule are all undisclosed. Post-hoc model selection, even within a pre-registered study, inflates the risk of false positives if the model form itself was not pre-specified.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: absence of power analysis
issues.description: The authors explicitly acknowledge that no statistical methods were used to determine sample size, and justify the chosen N by reference to comparably small prior studies. For the key between-treatment comparison (the paper's main theoretical test), 14 chains per treatment is small, and the resulting credible intervals are very wide. The justification 'our sample sizes are larger than those reported in previous publications' does not substitute for a power calculation and does not establish adequacy for the specific effect size of interest.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications.

issues.subcategory: missing individual-learning baseline control
issues.description: There is no condition in which participants optimize the wheel individually across 5 trials without receiving any social information from previous participants. Such a condition is necessary to establish how much improvement occurs from individual trial-and-error learning alone (without cultural transmission). Without this baseline, it is impossible to partition the observed generational improvement into individual learning versus true cultural accumulation via social information. The claim that social transmission drives improvement across generations rests on an unverified assumption.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track. All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain

issues.subcategory: behavioral prediction test does not operationalize explicit causal understanding
issues.description: The paper describes its measure as one of 'causal understanding,' but the test asks participants to predict which of two wheels will descend faster—a behavioral prediction task. This operationalization cannot distinguish explicit causal understanding (knowing that reduced moment of inertia causes faster rotation) from implicit empirical learning (having observed which configurations work through trial-and-error) or simple perceptual heuristics. The authors claim to 'rigorously measure participants' causal understanding,' but their instrument measures predictive accuracy, not causal knowledge. A valid causal understanding measure would require participants to generate explanations or make novel interventional predictions.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants' causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials… Participants were told that they would be presented with pairs of wheels and that they must guess which one of 2 wheels would descend the rails faster.

issues.subcategory: overclaim from low-dimensional task to complex multi-dimensional technology
issues.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the wheel task is 'low-dimensional,' providing 'a conservative test' relative to real technological optimization problems. Yet the conclusions claim that 'complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning.' The logic is not conservative: a finding that causal understanding is unnecessary for a two-variable problem does not straightforwardly extend to many-dimensional problems where selective, biased exploration (which the authors show is operating here) may be insufficient to traverse a much larger parameter space efficiently. The paper itself notes this distinction in the final results paragraph but does not retract the overclaim in the abstract and conclusions.
issues.quote: the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses… These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: credible intervals mislabeled as confidence intervals
issues.description: All analyses use Bayesian multilevel models with 95% credible intervals (HPDIs), yet the main results section refers to these as '95% Confidence Intervals.' Credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals have fundamentally different interpretations. The mislabeling is inconsistent with the stated methodology and potentially misleading to readers.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h… We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R

issues.subcategory: unanalyzed sex-segregated chain composition
issues.description: All chains were composed exclusively of one sex (7 all-male and 7 all-female chains per treatment). Sex differences in physics background, exploration strategy, or theory-generation tendencies could systematically affect the results. No analysis of sex differences is reported, and the design precludes examining sex as a within-treatment factor. This is particularly problematic given the paper's later claim (without data) that findings generalize to mixed-gender settings.
issues.quote: In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: maximum speed discrepancy between payoff formula and physics of system
issues.description: The payoff formula uses MaxSpeed = 160 m/h as the upper bound, but the paper states that 'the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h.' This discrepancy means the incentive structure was miscalibrated: participants could never achieve the payoff corresponding to MaxSpeed = 160, reducing the effective range of incentivization and meaning participants were always operating in a compressed portion of the payoff scale. The discrepancy also raises questions about whether the payoff parameters were set based on the actual physics of the system.
issues.quote: the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71%… with MaxSpeed = 160, MinSpeed = 96

issues.subcategory: payoff formula produces negative values for failed wheels
issues.description: The payoff formula assigns a speed of 0 to wheels that do not descend (as stated in Analysis 3), yielding a payoff of [1 − (160−0)/(160−96)] × 3 = −4.5 euros per failed trial. This creates a strong disincentive to explore configurations that might not work, potentially suppressing exactly the exploratory behavior the paper analyzes. Whether this penalty was applied or floored at zero in practice is not stated. The paper notes additional payments ranged from '0 and 26€,' suggesting a floor of zero, but this is never explicitly specified for the formula.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0… [1 - ((MaxSpeed – RecordedSpeed) / (MaxSpeed – MinSpeed))] x 3 + Bonus with MaxSpeed = 160, MinSpeed = 96

issues.subcategory: inconsistent treatment of failed trials across analyses
issues.description: Analysis 1 (Configurations treatment alone) restricts data to the last two trials 'to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset,' effectively excluding failures. Analysis 3 (between-treatment comparison) also restricts to the last two trials but additionally assigns speed = 0 to non-descending wheels. These are not equivalent approaches: the first removes failures from the outcome distribution while the second includes them as extreme low values, which could bias the between-treatment comparison in unpredictable ways depending on the distribution of failures across treatments and generations.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset [Analysis 1]… Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants' last two trials [Analysis 3]

issues.subcategory: theory quality across generations not reported
issues.description: The paper codes inherited theories by type (inertia, centre-of-mass, full, irrelevant) but never reports how theory accuracy or type distribution changed across generations within the Configurations + Theory treatment. This is a critical descriptive omission: if early chains tended to generate accurate theories that were transmitted faithfully, the conclusion about ineffectiveness of theory transmission would be very different than if early theories were predominantly inaccurate and biased later generations. The longitudinal dynamics of theory quality are essential context for interpreting the treatment comparison.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous chance-level baseline for understanding test
issues.description: The understanding test offers three response options ('Wheel 1,' 'Wheel 2,' 'No difference'), so the random-guessing expected score is 10/3 ≈ 3.33. However, a participant who has no causal knowledge but correctly infers that some wheel must be faster (from experimental context) would randomly choose between the two 'Wheel' options, yielding an expected score of 5.0. The figures show a 'horizontal line for random guessers' without specifying which chance level is used. The first-generation mean of 4.60 falls between these two chance baselines, making it unclear whether first-generation participants show above-chance understanding at all.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: 'Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2' or 'No difference'… Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.subcategory: different incentive structure for final-generation participants
issues.description: Final-generation participants had their last two payoffs doubled to compensate for not having a successor participant, but were not told this. This creates a generation-by-incentive-structure confound: final-generation participants operate under objectively different payoff conditions than all other participants, which could affect their optimization behavior. Since incentive magnitude affects exploration, and generation 5 is the generation whose performance is used to demonstrate cumulative improvement, this confound is directly relevant to the key result.
issues.quote: Final participants in chains had their last two payoffs doubled (although they were not aware of this as they didn't know that the chain was about to end).

issues.subcategory: unblinded data collection and analysis
issues.description: The experimenter physically positioned weights on the wheel based on participant configurations, while knowing which treatment the participant was assigned to. Although the physical task reduces scope for experimenter bias (wheel descent time is automatically recorded), subtle differences in weight placement precision could theoretically differ across conditions. More importantly, unblinded analysis of the exploratory components (theory coding aside, which used blind coders) introduces potential for confirmation bias.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: supplementary table numbering gap
issues.description: The methods section references Supplementary Tables 1, 2, 3, and 6 for Analyses 1–4 respectively. Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 are never mentioned in the main text. It is unclear what these tables contain or whether they are described in the supplementary materials. This gap in sequential numbering suggests either unreported analyses or tables referenced by the wrong numbers.
issues.quote: see Supplementary Table 3 for model output [Analysis 3]… see Supplementary Table 6 for model output [Analysis 4]

issues.subcategory: optimization percentage does not match stated values
issues.description: The paper reports '71% optimization after only four cultural generations.' Using the values provided (first generation mean = 123.6 m/h, fifth generation mean = 145.7 m/h, maximum = ~154 m/h), the calculation yields (145.7 − 123.6) / (154 − 123.6) = 22.1 / 30.4 ≈ 72.7%, not 71%. The discrepancy suggests either a rounding error, use of different values than those reported in the text, or an undisclosed baseline assumption. While minor in magnitude, this inconsistency undermines confidence in the accuracy of other reported calculations.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h… After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h… Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: fixed test question order introduces order effects
issues.description: All 140 participants completed the understanding test with the same 10 pairs of wheels presented in the same fixed sequence. This means any carryover or learning effects from earlier test items (e.g., noticing the pattern of correct answers, or inferring physics principles from the stimuli themselves) are systematically confounded with item position across all participants. Counterbalancing or randomizing question order would be standard practice to control for order effects.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.
